paragraphs.text: Estimation of adult height in the setting of tall parents or one tall parent is not entirely reliable. There are data to suggest that the Bayley-Pinneau (BP) method overesti mates, while the Tanner-Whitehouse (TW) method underestimates the predicted adult height in constitutionally tall children [2].
paragraphs.heading: Stature

paragraphs.text: If the child’s height prediction is in the range of the target adult height and there are no syndromic features, he/she most likely has familial tall stature. If the child grows or is projected to grow, beyond the target height range without syndromic fea tures or growth acceleration, hypoestro genism or estrogen resistance leading to delayed epiphyseal closure should be con sidered.
paragraphs.heading: Stature

paragraphs.text: Children and parents who find the predicted adult height unacceptable may seek treatment. However, there is little evidence that tall stat ure causes social or emotional challenges in adolescents or adults. Such therapy should be undertaken after an evaluation for hormonal causes of tall stature, as the latter may be treated by treating the underlying condition. Growth-reducing therapy is not commonly sought in patients with syndromic tall stature.
paragraphs.heading: Rate

paragraphs.text: Estrogen in high doses, such as 100–300 mcg of ethinyl estradiol daily, has been used in the past to accelerate growth plate maturation causing early epiphyseal fusion. The efficacy in reducing final height is better when treat ment is initiated at a lower bone age [2]. The mean height reduction is about 1.6 cm [3]. Long-term use of high-dose estrogen is linked with decreased fertility and increased inci dence of imminent ovarian failure [4, 5]. There is also concern for a higher risk of breast can cer [6] and thromboembolic episodes.
paragraphs.heading: 9.4.1 Sex Steroid Treatment

paragraphs.text: Testosterone treatment in boys is less effec tive than estrogen treatment in achieving final height reduction. It leads to early epiphyseal closure after aromatization to estrogen. There are studies showing equal efficacy of 250 and 500 mg of testosterone enanthate given intra muscularly every 2 weeks [7]. There are no known adverse effects on fertility or cancer risk in adolescents treated with high doses of
paragraphs.heading: 9.4.1 Sex Steroid Treatment

paragraphs.text: testosterone. However, high testosterone lev els may result in polycythemia and acne and cause aggressive behavior.
paragraphs.heading: 9.4.1 Sex Steroid Treatment

paragraphs.text: The most common surgical procedure used to decrease growth is bilateral percutaneous epi physiodesis of the distal femur and proximal tibia and fibula. In this operation, the growth plates of the long bones of the legs are obliter ated by needling to prevent more linear growth. Since this procedure decreases limb growth, it can potentially alter final body pro portions [8]. Unlike hormonal treatment, it can be used efficaciously at an advanced bone age. Complications are rare but include surgi cal scars, neurovascular damage, exostosis, or asymmetrical fusion leading to asymmetric limb length [9].
paragraphs.heading: 9.4.2 Surgery

paragraphs.text: Growth hormone (GH) excess is a very rare disorder of childhood. If it occurs in a grow ing child before epiphyseal fusion, it leads to tall stature causing gigantism. However, after epiphyseal fusion, GH excess has no effect on height and instead causes overgrowth of bone leading to acromegaly. Growth hormone excess can occur from a variety of sources— pituitary GH secretion from a tumor or somatotroph hyperplasia, hypothalamic GHreleasing hormone (GHRH) secretion, ecto pic source of GH or GHRH (extremely rare in children), or decrease in somatostatin inhi bition [10].
paragraphs.heading: 9.5 Growth Hormone Excess

paragraphs.text: This is a very rare disorder. The incidence of childhood pituitary tumors is about 0.1 in a million person-years, and less than 10% of these are GH-secreting adenomas [11, 12]. In a recent claims based approach in the United
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.1 Incidence

paragraphs.text: States that analyzed disease incidence based on acromegaly-based insurance claims, the annual incidence of GH excess in children, from 2008 to 2012, was three to eight cases per million person-years. There was no significant difference between incidence based on gender and the incidence increased with increasing age [13].
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.1 Incidence

paragraphs.text: The usual presentation of growth hormone excess before epiphyseal fusion is increased growth velocity and tall stature. In older ado lescents, musculoskeletal symptoms of GH excess, i.e., arthralgias, wrist pain, large feet and hands, coarsening of facial features, prog nathism, macrocephaly, and kyphoscoliosis, may be seen. Sleep apnea from mucosal and lymphoid hypertrophy may occur. Complications of GH excess such as hyper tension, cardiomyopathy, glucose intolerance, or frank diabetes mellitus are less often seen in this younger age group.

paragraphs.text: The goal of the treatment is to (a) remove or shrink the tumor, (b) normalize GH secretion and IGF-1 levels while preserving pituitary function to avoid long-term complications, and (c) decrease the morbidity and mortality associated with GH excess. As with most pitu itary tumors, younger age at presentation is associated with more aggressive tumors [24]. Giant GH-secreting pituitary tumors are invasive and need a multimodal treatment approach to control GH excess and tumor growth [25]. Surgery is the mainstay of ther apy, but adjuvant medical and radiation ther apy are often needed. There is debate in the literature about the relative importance of normalization of the IGF-1 level versus nadir GH levels after glucose suppression in pre dicting better outcomes [26–28]. Of note, much of the data come from older patients with acromegaly and should be interpreted

paragraphs.heading: 9.5.4 Treatment

paragraphs.text: Medical therapy is sometimes used preopera tively to reduce IGF-1 levels and for tumor shrinkage for better surgical outcomes. It is also needed postoperatively for biochemical control if remission does not occur with surgi cal and radiation therapy.
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.4.1 Medical Therapy

paragraphs.text: There are two analogs available in the mar ket—long-acting release octreotide (LAR) given intramuscularly and lanreotide depot/ autogel given subcutaneously. They have a greater affinity for somatostatin type 2 (sst2) and type 5 (sst5) receptors found in the pan creas, pituitary gland, and GH-secreting neo plasms of the pituitary gland, and a lesser affinity for somatostatin receptors 1, 3, and 4. Both preparations are equally effective at reducing IGF-1 levels [29].
paragraphs.heading: Somatostatin Analogs (SSTA)

paragraphs.text: Pasireotide is another somatostatin analog with enhanced binding to more somatostatin receptors. Pasireotide binds to somatostatin receptors (sst1–5), with high affinity for the sst1, sst2, and sst3 subtypes and the highest affinity for the sst5 subtype. Its diverse receptor bind ing allows for its use in both Cushing’s disease and conditions of GH excess. In vitro studies suggest similar decreases in GH levels with first-generation SSTAs and pasireotide [30].
paragraphs.heading: Somatostatin Analogs (SSTA)

paragraphs.text: The response to SSTA correlates with the expression of sst2 receptors [31], but receptor expression is not routinely assessed clinically. Smaller tumors, lower baseline IGF-1, and densely granulated tumors which appear hypointense on T2-weighted MRI images show a better response to SSRA [32, 33]. IGF-1 normalization is achieved in both drug naive and postoperative patients in about 20–35% of patients, and about 50% reduction in tumor volume is obtained in about 59% of patients [34, 35].
paragraphs.heading: Somatostatin Analogs (SSTA)

paragraphs.text: Dosing and Side Effects Lanreotide depot (starting dose of 60–120 mg every 4 weeks depending on IGF-1 level) and
paragraphs.heading: Somatostatin Analogs (SSTA)

paragraphs.text: long-acting octreotide (10–40 mg every 4 weeks) should be slowly titrated up until a normal IGF-1 level is attained. Abdominal cramps, flatulence, and diarrhea can be severe leading to discontinuation of treatment in some individuals, but the medications are typ ically well tolerated. Since the medications are depot preparations and these side effects can be severe, a trial of a short-acting preparation may be used to establish tolerance before starting treatment with the long-acting prepa ration. These medications can also be associated with gallstone disease, which is usually seen in the first few years of treatment. Long-acting pasireotide is also available and can be used at a dose of 20–60 mg every 4 weeks. Pasireotide may cause hyperglycemia as it inhibits insulin secretion in more than half of all patients [36]. Pasireotide may be effective in some patients uncontrolled on lan reotide [37, 38]. Delayed-release oral octreo tide capsules are available for long-term maintenance treatment in those who responded to and tolerated octreotide or lan reotide [39].
paragraphs.heading: Somatostatin Analogs (SSTA)

paragraphs.text: Dopamine agonists are usually used alone (for mild IGF-1 elevations) or in conjunction with an SSTA, and the combination may be effective in lowering the IGF-1 level further [40]. The response to dopamine agonists is independent of the baseline prolactin levels or histochemical staining of the tumor for pro lactin [41, 42]. The efficacy of cabergoline appears to decrease with its prolonged use [42]. The valvular side effects associated with cumulative cabergoline use do not seem to be exaggerated in patients with GH excess [43].
paragraphs.heading: Dopamine Agonists

paragraphs.text: Pegvisomant is a GH receptor antagonist that blocks the peripheral production of IGF-1 in a dose-dependent manner. As pegvisomant does not inhibit GH secretion, GH levels con tinue to be elevated during pegvisomant administration. The medication can lead to an increase in adenoma size and radiological monitoring should be considered [44–46]. The
paragraphs.heading: Growth Hormone Receptor Antagonist (Pegvisomant)

paragraphs.text: combination of pegvisomant with an SSTA and dopamine agonist is more effective than either drug used alone [47]. Pegvisomant is administered as daily subcutaneous injec tions, which may have an impact on adherence to therapy. Common side effects include local discomfort and lipohypertrophy. Elevations in transaminases are seen in a very small subset of patients, and the medication should be withheld if the elevation is greater than three times the upper limit of the normal range [48]. Liver function tests should be checked monthly for the first 6 months after initiating pegvisomant and then every 6 months if toler ated well. Acrostudy, which has 10-year fol low-up data, showed that three-quarter of patients achieve biochemical control with pegvisomant and it may improve glucose metabolism in those with diabetes mellitus [49, 50].
paragraphs.heading: Growth Hormone Receptor Antagonist (Pegvisomant)

paragraphs.text: This is the treatment of choice for small as well as large tumors that are resectable and those that pose a risk of visual loss. The cure rate depends on the size of the tumor and the expertise of the surgeon [51]. When operated in a center with a high volume of surgery by one or more experienced pituitary surgeons, the initial remission rate for microadenomas can be more than 85% and almost 50% for macroadenomas [52]. Tumor invasion into the cavernous sinus decreases the remission rate [53]. There is an immediate lowering of GH levels with successful surgery; however, the decline in IGF-1 may sometimes be delayed due to the differential half-life of its binding proteins. Hence, the IGF-1 level assessed about 12 weeks after surgery may be a better reflection of surgical success than an earlier level [54, 55].
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.4.2 Surgical Therapy

paragraphs.text: This serves as adjuvant therapy when there is a residual tumor after surgery. Radiotherapy leads to a decrease in tumor size and reduces IGF-1 concentrations in the majority of patients [56]. However, radiation effects may take a few years to manifest, and hence this is
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.4.3 Radiation Therapy

paragraphs.text: used in situations where both surgery and medical therapy are not effective in treating the condition, and not as a primary therapy [57]. Stereotactic radiotherapy aims to deliver radiation in a more precise manner and may have fewer complications [58]. The increased availability and use of proton beam radiation therapy allow for more targeted delivery of radiation to the tumor with less radiation scatter and hence fewer side effects of radia tion. Patients who receive radiation should be monitored for other pituitary deficiencies, which may evolve over the next decade.
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.4.3 Radiation Therapy

paragraphs.text: Many of the complications associated with long-term exposure to GH excess are not wit nessed by pediatric endocrinologists. However, there is increased morbidity and mortality associated with this disorder in adults.
paragraphs.heading: Complications

paragraphs.text: Data regarding the cure rate after surgery (not needing medical therapy) are difficult to inter pret due to the variable duration of follow-up and different biochemical cut-offs used to define cure. The early remission rate after sur gery is about 80% in microadenomas and less than 50% with macroadenomas [59, 60]. About 40% of patients who achieve remission postoperatively have normal GH levels 16 years after surgery [60].
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.5.1 Cure and Remission

paragraphs.text: Mortality with prolonged GH excess is higher than in the general population [61]. The main cause of mortality a decade ago was cardiovascular mortality; however, more neoplastic processes contributing to mortal ity have been reported in recent years [62, 63]. Mortality is also linked to higher GH and IGF-1 levels at the end of life [63]. With the advent of better medical therapies, the pro portion of patients with biochemically con trolled disease has increased leading to improved outcomes [64].
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.5.2 Mortality

paragraphs.text: This may result from residual tumor compres sion, surgical, and/or radiation treatment. This needs monitoring at least on an annual basis, or earlier in case of symptoms sugges tive of pituitary hormone deficiencies.
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.5.3 Panhypopituitarism

paragraphs.text: GH excess is associated with cardiomyopa thy—biventricular hypertrophy, hypertension, valvulopathies, and endothelial dysfunction [65]. Hypertension is seen in almost half of the patients [66]. Reversal of the cardiac defects can be achieved with appropriate bio chemical control and is dependent on patient age, disease duration, and other metabolic comorbidities [67].
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.5.4 Cardiovascular

paragraphs.text: The anatomical changes in soft tissues, mucosa, lymphoid tissue, and the skeleton including tongue swelling, rib cage deformity, and changes in lung volume and elasticity can result in disordered sleep and decreased respi ratory reserve. Sleep apnea may persist after recovery from GH excess, and hence polysom nography should be considered in high-risk patients with overweight and diabetes [68].
paragraphs.heading: Disorders

paragraphs.text: Abnormalities in glucose metabolism can range from impaired glucose tolerance to impaired fasting glucose to frank diabetes, and the prevalence is higher than that seen in the general population [69]. Chronic GH excess leads to insulin resistance at the hepatic and peripheral tissue levels (muscle and adi pose tissue) [70]. Some therapies, particularly
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.5.6 Glucose Metabolism

paragraphs.text: pasireotide, are known to worsen glucose tol erance. Hyperglycemia may persist even after GH excess is cured [71].
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.5.6 Glucose Metabolism

paragraphs.text: There is increased recognition of the higher prevalence of vertebral fractures in patients with GH excess, which correlates with disease activity [72]. More research is necessary to predict fracture risk in this population, which happens in the setting of normal bone min eral density [73].
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.5.7 Bone Outcomes

paragraphs.text: Benign and malignant neoplasms are more common in GH excess patients compared to an age-matched population. Colonic polyps are the most common type of tumor seen with GH excess [74]. There is a fivefold increased risk of thyroid cancer [75]. The increased risk of colon, breast, and prostate cancer in acro megaly as compared to the general population is currently a matter of debate [76–78]. While some groups think that acromegaly increases the risk of these neoplasms, others doubt this supposition as cancer-related mortality is lower in acromegaly compared with the gen eral population [79, 80]. Nonetheless, until proven otherwise, systematic screening for a neoplastic disease is advised in older patients.
paragraphs.heading: 9.5.5.8 Neoplasia

paragraphs.text: QoL is impaired in patients with GH excess despite improvement in the disease state. However, biochemical control is shown to improve QoL [81]. Other factors, including obesity, depression, fatigue, and metabolic complications, should be taken into account when addressing QoL in this population.

As with most pitu itary tumors, younger age at presentation is associated with more aggressive tumors [24]. Giant GH-secreting pituitary tumors are invasive and need a multimodal treatment approach to control GH excess and tumor growth [25]. Surgery is the mainstay of ther apy, but adjuvant medical and radiation ther apy are often needed. There is debate in the literature about the relative importance of normalization of the IGF-1 level versus nadir GH levels after glucose suppression in pre dicting better outcomes [26–28]. Pasireotide binds to somatostatin receptors (sst1–5), with high affinity for the sst1, sst2, and sst3 subtypes and the highest affinity for the sst5 subtype. Its diverse receptor bind ing allows for its use in both Cushing’s disease and conditions of GH excess. In vitro studies suggest similar decreases in GH levels with first-generation SSTAs and pasireotide [30]. The response to SSTA correlates with the expression of sst2 receptors [31], but receptor expression is not routinely assessed clinically. The cure rate depends on the size of the tumor and the expertise of the surgeon [51].
